cards.definition: Change directory: moves your shell into another directory. With no argument it takes you home.
cards.useCase: Move around the file system. Relative paths start from where you are; absolute paths start at /.

cards.definition: A single dot is the current directory and two dots are its parent. So cd .. goes up a level, and cd . stays put.
cards.useCase: Go up one level with ..; the single dot is handy in commands such as cp file . (copy it here).

cards.definition: Print working directory: shows the full path of the directory you are in.
cards.useCase: Check where you are before using a relative path or deleting anything.

cards.definition: Lists the files and directories in a directory.
cards.useCase: See what is here. Options change how much detail you get and in what order.

cards.definition: Long listing: file type and permissions, link count, owner, group, size, date and name for each entry.
cards.useCase: Check permissions and ownership.

cards.definition: A long listing (-l) sorted by modification time (-t), with the order reversed (-r), so the oldest file is first and the newest is last.
cards.useCase: The most recently changed file ends up at the bottom, next to your prompt.

cards.definition: Prints the name of the account you are logged in as.
cards.useCase: Check who you are before running privileged commands.

cards.definition: Switch user. With no name it switches to root, loads root's login environment, and asks for root's password.
cards.useCase: Get a root shell, or become another user with su - name. Type exit to come back.

cards.definition: Runs a single command with root privileges, if the sudoers configuration allows you. It asks for your own password.
cards.useCase: Do administration without staying logged in as root.
cards.example:
sudo ls /root
sudo systemctl restart sshd

cards.definition: Uses sudo to run su, which gives you a root shell. You type your own password, not root's.
cards.useCase: A quick way to become root when your account is allowed to use sudo.

cards.definition: Clears the terminal screen.
cards.useCase: Tidy up the display. Ctrl+L does the same thing.

cards.definition: Displays the manual page for a command: its options, syntax and examples.
cards.useCase: Look something up without leaving the terminal. Press q to quit and / to search the page.

cards.definition: Copies a file to a new name or location. With -r it copies a directory and everything in it.
cards.useCase: Make a backup or a duplicate. The original stays where it is.
cards.example:
cp notes.txt notes.bak
cp -r project project-backup

cards.definition: Moves a file or directory somewhere else. Moving within the same directory is how you rename.
cards.useCase: Rename or relocate files.

cards.definition: Removes (deletes) files. There is no trash can, so deleted files are gone.
cards.useCase: Delete files you no longer need. Add -i to be asked before each one.

cards.definition: Makes a new directory.
cards.useCase: Create folders. With -p it also creates any missing parent directories.

cards.definition: Removes a directory, but only if it is empty. It refuses if anything is inside.
cards.useCase: Safe cleanup of empty folders.

cards.definition: Removes a directory and everything inside it, working recursively.
cards.useCase: Delete a folder that is not empty, where rmdir would refuse.

cards.definition: Recursive (-r) and forced (-f) removal: deletes a whole tree without prompting and ignores files that do not exist.
cards.useCase: Very powerful and very dangerous. Double-check the path before pressing Enter.

cards.definition: Creates an empty file if it does not exist yet, or updates its timestamp if it does.
cards.useCase: Make placeholder files quickly, especially together with brace expansion.

cards.definition: Changes the permission bits (read, write, execute) of a file or directory, in symbolic or octal form.
cards.useCase: Make a script executable, or lock a file down.

cards.definition: Changes the owner of a file, and optionally its group too (owner:group).
cards.useCase: Hand a file over to another user. Needs root.
cards.example:
sudo chown alice report.txt
sudo chown alice:staff report.txt

cards.definition: Changes the group that owns a file.
cards.useCase: Share files with a team without changing the owner.

cards.definition: Each permission has a number: read is 4, write is 2, execute is 1. You add them up separately for the owner, the group and others.
cards.useCase: Convert quickly: 7 = rwx, 6 = rw-, 5 = r-x, 4 = r--, 0 = no access.

cards.definition: Owner rwx, group r-x, others r-x. The usual mode for programs and directories.
cards.useCase: Everyone can run it or enter it, but only the owner can change it.

cards.definition: Owner rw-, group r--, others r--. The usual mode for ordinary files.
cards.useCase: Everyone can read it, only the owner can edit it.

cards.definition: Owner rw-, and no access at all for the group or others.
cards.useCase: Private files, such as SSH keys.

cards.definition: Symbolic mode: u is the owner, + adds a permission, x is execute. All the other bits stay as they are.
cards.useCase: Make a script runnable without touching its other permissions. Use g or o for group or others, - to remove.
cards.example:
chmod u+x script.sh
chmod g-w file.txt

cards.definition: Ten characters: the file type, then rwx for the owner, the group and others. A dash means that permission is missing.
cards.useCase: Work out who can do what from a long listing.
cards.example:
-rwxr-xr--  1 alice staff 120 notes.sh
(file; owner rwx; group r-x; others r--)

cards.definition: Matches zero or more characters in a file name.
cards.useCase: Act on many files at once. Note that it also matches nothing, so project* matches plain project.

cards.definition: Matches exactly one character.
cards.useCase: Match names of a fixed length: one ? is one character, two ?? are two.
cards.example:
ls project?     # project1, projectA
ls project??    # project12

cards.definition: Matches exactly one character from the listed set or range.
cards.useCase: Pick out particular names: [aegh] is a list, [a-h] is a range.

cards.definition: A set starting with ! matches one character that is NOT any of those listed.
cards.useCase: Match everything except a few characters.

cards.definition: The shell expands {...} lists and ranges into separate words before the command runs. It builds names; it does not search for files that exist.
cards.useCase: Create many files or directories in one command.

cards.definition: Prints a file's contents to the screen.
cards.useCase: Look at a short file, or feed a file into a pipe.

cards.definition: Prints a file with the last line first. It is cat spelled backwards.
cards.useCase: Read a log from newest to oldest.

cards.definition: Shows a file one screen at a time. Press Space for the next page.
cards.useCase: Page through a long file or a long command output.

cards.definition: A pager that can also scroll backwards and search. Arrow keys or j and k move a line at a time, / searches, q quits.
cards.useCase: Read long files comfortably. Usually better than more.

cards.definition: Shows the first 10 lines of a file, or as many as you ask for with -n.
cards.useCase: Peek at the start of a file.

cards.definition: Shows the last 10 lines of a file. With -f it keeps following new lines as they are added.
cards.useCase: Check the latest log entries.

cards.definition: A simple text editor that shows its key commands on screen. Ctrl+O saves and Ctrl+X exits.
cards.useCase: Quick edits without learning vi.

cards.definition: Lists who is logged in right now, with their terminal and login time.
cards.useCase: See who else is on the system.

cards.definition: Shows who is logged in and what each person is running, plus the system load.
cards.useCase: A fuller view than who.

cards.definition: Shows the history of logins and reboots, newest first.
cards.useCase: Find out who logged in, from where, and when.

cards.definition: Prints a short summary of users: login name, real name, terminal, idle time and login time. It may need to be installed.
cards.useCase: Look up information about a user.

cards.definition: Shows your user ID, your group ID and all the groups you belong to, or those of another user.
cards.useCase: Check group membership, for example whether you are in wheel.

cards.definition: Displays the system date and time. As root it can also set them with -s.
cards.useCase: Check the clock, or set it before testing a scheduled job.

cards.definition: Shows how long the system has been running, how many users are logged in, and the load average.
cards.useCase: Find out when the machine last rebooted and how busy it is.

cards.definition: Shows (or sets) the name of the machine.
cards.useCase: Confirm which server you are on.

cards.definition: Prints information about the kernel and operating system. -r gives the kernel release and -a gives everything.
cards.useCase: Check the kernel version.

cards.definition: Shows the full path of the program that would run for a command name.
cards.useCase: Find where a command lives.

cards.definition: Displays a calendar for this month, a given month, or a whole year.
cards.useCase: Check a date quickly.

cards.definition: A command-line calculator for basic arithmetic.
cards.useCase: Do sums in the terminal, or pipe an expression into it.

cards.definition: Controls systemd services: start, stop, restart, enable at boot, and show status. It replaced the service command in RHEL 7. Most actions need root.
cards.useCase: Start a service now, or make it start automatically at boot.
cards.example:
sudo systemctl start httpd
sudo systemctl enable httpd
systemctl status httpd

cards.definition: The older command for starting and stopping services. On current RHEL it is a thin wrapper around systemctl.
cards.useCase: Recognize it in older tutorials and scripts.

cards.definition: Lists processes. On its own it shows only your current shell; the options aux show every process.
cards.useCase: Find a process and its ID.

cards.definition: A live, updating view of processes with their CPU and memory use. Press q to quit.
cards.useCase: See what is using the machine's resources right now.

cards.definition: Sends a signal to a process, by its ID. The default asks it to terminate; -9 forces it.
cards.useCase: Stop a stuck program. An ordinary user can only signal their own processes.

cards.definition: Summarizes memory: total, used and free RAM, and swap. -h shows human-readable sizes.
cards.useCase: Check whether the machine is short of memory.

cards.definition: Reports free disk space for each mounted file system. -h shows human-readable sizes.
cards.useCase: Find out which disk is filling up.

cards.definition: Prints the kernel's message buffer: hardware detection, driver messages, warnings and errors.
cards.useCase: Diagnose hardware or boot problems.

cards.definition: Reports CPU and disk input/output statistics. A number gives the refresh interval in seconds. It is part of the sysstat package.
cards.useCase: Watch disk activity over time.

cards.definition: Shows network connections, listening ports, the routing table and interface statistics. An older tool, now replaced by ss and ip.
cards.useCase: See what the machine is connected to and what it is listening on.

cards.definition: A virtual file the kernel generates that describes each CPU.
cards.useCase: Check the processor model and number of cores.

cards.definition: A virtual file the kernel generates that describes memory use in detail.
cards.useCase: See the numbers behind the free command.

cards.definition: Searches a directory tree for files by name, type, size, owner and more. It reads the real directories each time, so it is always up to date.
cards.useCase: Locate a file when you know part of its name. The first argument is where to start.

cards.definition: Finds files by name using a prebuilt database. Very fast, but only as current as the last updatedb run.
cards.useCase: A quick lookup for files that have existed for a while.

cards.definition: A second name for the same data. Deleting, renaming or moving the original does not affect it, and the data stays until the last name is gone.
cards.useCase: Keep a file reachable under two names within one file system.

cards.definition: A small file that stores the path to its target, like a shortcut. If the target is deleted or renamed, the link breaks.
cards.useCase: Point to a file or directory somewhere else, even on another file system.

cards.definition: ln makes a hard link. ln -s makes a soft (symbolic) link.
cards.useCase: Pick the link type: -s when you want a shortcut that can cross file systems.
cards.example:
ln file hardlink
ln -s file softlink

cards.definition: Redirects a command's output into a file, replacing whatever was in the file.
cards.useCase: Save output. Be careful: an existing file is wiped.

cards.definition: Redirects output to the end of a file, keeping what is already there.
cards.useCase: Add to a log or list.

cards.definition: Sends the output of one command to the input of the next.
cards.useCase: Chain small tools together.

cards.definition: Prints the lines that match a pattern. -c counts them, -i ignores case.
cards.useCase: Search inside files or command output.
cards.example:
grep Cat animals
grep -c Cat animals

cards.definition: Sorts lines of text. -n sorts numerically, -r reverses, -k picks a column.
cards.useCase: Put output in order, and prepare it for uniq.

cards.definition: Collapses repeated lines, but only when they are next to each other, so the input should be sorted first. -c counts them.
cards.useCase: Remove duplicates or count them.

cards.definition: The standard counting pipeline: sort puts identical lines together, then uniq -c counts each group.
cards.useCase: Build a frequency table of anything.

cards.definition: Processes text one line at a time, split into fields: $1 is the first field, $2 the second, and so on.
cards.useCase: Pull out a column.

cards.definition: A stream editor. The common use is substitution: s/old/new/ replaces the first match on each line.
cards.useCase: Find and replace in text without opening an editor.

cards.definition: Copies its input to a file and also passes it on to the screen (or the next command).
cards.useCase: Save an intermediate result while still seeing it.

cards.definition: Counts lines, words and bytes. -l counts lines only.
cards.useCase: Count how many lines or matches there are.
cards.example:
wc -l animals
grep Cat animals | wc -l

cards.definition: Creates a new user account. adduser is the same command on RHEL and CentOS. New accounts are locked until a password is set.
cards.useCase: Add someone to the system.

cards.definition: Sets or changes a user's password. Weak passwords may be rejected by the dictionary check.
cards.useCase: Unlock a new account, or reset a password.

cards.definition: Creates a new group.
cards.useCase: Set up a group before adding users to it.

cards.definition: Modifies an existing user account: groups, shell, home directory and more.
cards.useCase: Change a user without recreating them.

cards.definition: -G sets a user's supplementary groups and -a appends to them. Without -a, the user's other supplementary groups are replaced.
cards.useCase: Add a user to a group safely. Never leave out the -a.

cards.definition: On RHEL and CentOS, members of this special group may run any command as root through sudo.
cards.useCase: The way to make an account an administrator.

cards.definition: Starts a login session as another user. As root you do not need their password. exit returns to your own session.
cards.useCase: Test a new account.

cards.definition: A quick test that sudo works: it prints root, because the command ran with root's rights.
cards.useCase: Verify that a new sudo user was set up correctly.

cards.term: Steps to add a sudo user
cards.definition: Become root, create the user, set a password, add the user to wheel, then test with su - and sudo.
cards.useCase: The complete recipe, in order.
cards.example:
sudo su
useradd newuser
passwd newuser
usermod -aG wheel newuser
su - newuser
sudo whoami

cards.definition: The configuration file that decides who may use sudo. Edit it with visudo, which checks the syntax. On RHEL the wheel group is granted full access.
cards.useCase: See where sudo permissions come from.

cards.definition: vi starts in command mode, where keys are commands rather than text. Press i to enter insert mode and type; Esc returns to command mode.
cards.useCase: The reason typing appears to do nothing when you first open a file.

cards.definition: Enters insert mode, so what you type goes into the file.
cards.useCase: Start adding text at the cursor.

cards.definition: Leaves insert mode and returns to command mode.
cards.useCase: The way out of any mode.

cards.definition: Replaces the single character under the cursor with the next one you type.
cards.useCase: Fix one wrong letter.

cards.definition: Deletes the current line.
cards.useCase: Remove a whole line quickly.

cards.definition: Undoes the last change.
cards.useCase: Recover from a mistaken delete.

cards.definition: Deletes the character under the cursor.
cards.useCase: Remove a single character.

cards.definition: Quits without saving, throwing away any changes.
cards.useCase: Get out after a mistake.

cards.definition: Both save the file and quit. ZZ is Shift+Z pressed twice, from command mode.
cards.useCase: Finish editing and keep your changes.

cards.definition: Searches forward for a string. Press n for the next match.
cards.useCase: Find a word in a long file.

cards.definition: Edits your personal cron table, normally in vi. Each line is one scheduled job.
cards.useCase: Schedule a command or script to run automatically.

cards.definition: -l lists your scheduled jobs and -r removes all of them. As root, -u name works on another user's table.
cards.useCase: Check what is scheduled, or clear it. Be careful: -r deletes the whole table.

cards.definition: A cron line is: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week, then the command. A * means every value.
cards.useCase: Read any schedule from left to right.
cards.example:
30 16 2 * *  /path/script.sh
# 4:30 p.m. on the 2nd of every month

cards.definition: Minute 0, hour 3, every day, every month, every weekday: runs daily at 3:00 a.m.
cards.useCase: A typical nightly job such as a backup.

cards.definition: */n means every n units of that field. A range like 1-5 covers several values; in the weekday field 1-5 is Monday to Friday.
cards.useCase: Repeat often, or run only on weekdays.

cards.definition: Shortcuts for common schedules: @hourly (0 * * * *), @daily or @midnight (0 0 * * *), @weekly (0 0 * * 0), @monthly (0 0 1 * *), @yearly (0 0 1 1 *), @reboot (once at startup).
cards.useCase: Write a schedule without counting stars.

cards.definition: The first line of a script. It names the interpreter that should run the file.
cards.useCase: Tell the system which shell the script is written for.

cards.definition: bash script reads it, so it only needs read permission. ./script runs it directly, so it needs execute permission (and the shebang).
cards.useCase: Choose how to launch a script.

cards.definition: Runs commands only when a test is true. The test goes in [ ] with spaces inside, and the block ends with fi.
cards.useCase: Make a decision, such as whether a file exists.

cards.definition: Repeats commands once for each value in a list, setting a variable each time. The body is closed with done.
cards.useCase: Do the same thing to several items.
cards.example:
for name in alice bob carol; do
  echo "Hello, $name"
done

cards.definition: Chooses between several patterns. Each branch ends with ;; and the whole statement is closed with esac.
cards.useCase: A tidy alternative to a long chain of ifs.
